chunks: Advantages of open-drain outputs. The question: What are advantages of the open-drain output drivers?
An open-drain output can only pull a wire down to ground or let go of it. It can never push the wire up.
A resistor to the supply, called a pull-up, brings the wire back up when everyone lets go. This sounds like a limit, but it is what lets many chips share one wire safely.
If two chips disagree, "low" simply wins and nothing is harmed.
Picture a cord held up by a spring, with several people each holding a handle. Anyone can pull the cord down. Nobody ever pushes it up.
When all of them let go, the spring lifts it. Two people pulling down never fight each other. The analogy shows the cost too: a spring lifts slowly, while pulling down is quick.
That is why this kind of wire is slow to go high.
Dashed segments mean "released" (the pull-up is providing the level). Whenever either device pulls low the bus is 0; it's 1 only when both release.
No time slot exists where two outputs fight.
Open-drain: an output with only a pull-down switch. It pulls low or lets go. Push-pull: an output with two switches, one that drives high and one that drives low.
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts the wire high when nobody pulls it low. Contention: two outputs driving opposite levels at once, so current flows straight through both.
Wired-AND: a shared wire that is high only if every chip lets go.
Two chips share a wire on a 3. 3 volts supply. Suppose both were push-pull, and one drives high while the other drives low.
Current flows from supply to ground through both switches. If those switches have about 25 ohms and 20 ohms, that is 3. 3 over 45 about 73 milliamps. That can damage the chips.
Now make both open-drain with a 2. 2 kilohms pull-up. The worst case is the pull-up current through a chip pulling low: 3. 3 over 2200 equals 1. 5 milliamps.
That is the whole idea.
"Open-drain outputs can only pull low; a pull-up makes the high.
That gives a wired-AND, so devices can share a wire without contention: if two disagree, low simply wins, instead of a shoot-through current between a PMOS and an NMOS.
It's what enables I2C's arbitration, clock stretching and ACK. It also makes level mixing easy and tolerates hot-plug.
The cost is a slow rising edge set by R pC b and static current when the line is low."
